cim: Building Trust in Artificial Intelligence, One Install at a Time
cim_eredeti: Building Trust in Artificial Intelligence, One Install at a Time
szoveg_eredeti:
By now, most security integrators have sat across from a customer who has read about artificial intelligence (AI), seen a demo and wants to know what it can do for their site.

AI technology is moving fast enough that much of what gets promised today will look different in a year. What won’t change is who the customer calls when a system doesn’t work, or works in a way nobody expected, and that’s the integrator.

Intelligent new tools are great. So are guardrails around the use of them. Manufacturers, integrators and end customers all share responsibility for how AI is deployed. Because integrators design the system, set it up and stand behind it, they’re best placed to turn good intentions into practical guardrails.

This step protects the customer relationship, because nobody should deliver technology in a way that leaves the customer regretting their decision.

Strong guardrails start with the customer’s problem, not the tool’s capabilities and alarms are a good example. False alarms are one of the industry’s oldest problems and the operator fatigue that comes with them is just as costly.

One large organization I know of routinely ignores about 20 alarm types because they come in too often to answer. AI that checks each alarm against the camera view can filter out that noise and show operators what matters.

The next step is letting AI act on its own, such as clearing a false alarm, and each customer will need to decide how much to hand over. But before any of it goes live, the integrator needs to prove the AI works specifically on the customer’s site, because accuracy in a vendor demo is not the same as accuracy in a parking lot at night or in the rain. An on-site pilot with measured results protects the customer’s budget and the integrator’s reputation.

That proof starts before the pilot, with the questions integrators ask vendors. Customers rarely have the time or background to test every AI claim themselves, so they count on their integrator to do it for them.

A few direct questions early in an evaluation can save months of frustration later and they belong in every conversation with a vendor:

A security vendor that answers these questions clearly is easier to recommend and one that can’t provide clear answers is telling you something as well.

Privacy tools are a natural place to start the risk conversation, and most customers already know blur and redaction. Blur obscures people by default, with authorized unblur when there’s a legitimate need, and redaction removes bystanders before video is shared with police, courts, insurers or the media.

Fewer customers have considered anonymization, which alters identifying features so the video still looks natural but no one in it can be identified. Together, these tools make it easier for legal, HR and privacy teams to approve a project, and harder for a single shared clip to become a liability.

Keeping people in the decision process protects the organization in much the same way, especially as AI takes on more of the work. Operators should understand what a system will do before it acts, because a person who only clicks “yes” isn’t much of a safeguard.

Security integrators can also build in an audit trail that shows what the AI recommended and who approved it so, if a decision is ever questioned, the customer and the integrator both have the record to back it up.

It’s important to recognize that AI will keep changing at speed and not every tool will live up to its promise. What can stay steady is how the channel handles that change. Manufacturers owe integrators honest claims and transparent development, integrators owe customers clear answers and systems built with guardrails and customers owe the public responsible use.

When every part of the channel does its share, nobody ends up regretting the decision and the technology does what it should: serving people rather than the other way around.

Tim Palmquist is vice president of the Americas at Milestone Systems.
